title: Microprogrammed Control: The Control Store and the Microinstruction
quickIdea: Instead of wiring the control signals, write each control word into a memory. The unit then has two jobs: read a word out and put its bits on the control lines, which is trivial, and work out which word to read next, which is the whole design.
remember: Control store (control memory): a ROM or writable RAM holding every microinstruction of every instruction's routine.
Control address register (CAR, also written micro-PC): holds the address of the microinstruction being fetched.
Control data register (CDR, also written micro-IR or pipeline register): holds the microinstruction just read, so its bits can drive the control lines while the next address is computed.
A microinstruction is one control word plus, usually, the bits that say how to find the next one.
A microprogram is the sequence of microinstructions for one machine instruction; a microroutine is that sequence for one phase.
The idea is Wilkes's, published in 1951; EDSAC 2 in 1958 was the first machine built with a microprogrammed control unit.

example.prompt: A control store holds 128 microinstructions of 20 bits. How many bits does it hold, and what does each register in the unit hold?
example.work: 128 x 20 = 2560 bits. The CAR holds a 7-bit address (2^7 = 128). The CDR holds one 20-bit microinstruction. The datapath receives the control-signal bits of that word directly.
example.answer: 2560 bits of control store, a 7-bit control address register and a 20-bit control data register.

gateAngle: Two things are asked: the size arithmetic (words times width) and the role of each register. The distinction that decides questions is that the CAR addresses the store and the CDR holds the word - swapping them is the standard wrong answer. GATE CSE 2004 Q.67 is exactly the size arithmetic, done on a 26-bit word.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: Why does a microprogrammed unit need a control data register at all, when the control word could drive the lines straight out of memory?
variations.answer: So the word stays stable on the control lines while the next address is computed and the next word is fetched; without it the control lines would change as soon as the memory output changed.
variations.why: It is a pipeline register: it holds this word while the store is read for the next. Some designs omit it and accept that the store's read time is part of every clock.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: What is the difference between a microinstruction and a machine instruction?
variations.answer: A machine instruction is what the programmer writes and the decoder recognises; a microinstruction is one internal step of executing it, held in the control store and never visible to the program.
variations.why: One machine instruction becomes several microinstructions, so microprogramming sits a level below the instruction set - which is why the two are confused in prose but never in hardware.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: A control store of 512 words holds 40-bit microinstructions. How many bits is the CAR, and how many control signals could the word drive horizontally?
variations.answer: 9 bits for the CAR (2^9 = 512), and up to 40 signals if every bit were used horizontally - in practice some bits are spent on sequencing.
variations.why: The address width comes from the word count, the word width from the signal count plus sequencing, and the two are independent.

trap.what: Assuming that because the control word is stored, the unit no longer needs the opcode.
trap.why: The opcode is still needed, but only once per instruction: to find the start of that instruction's microprogram. After the jump, the sequencing comes from the microinstruction's own fields.
trap.counterexample: Without the opcode the unit could not choose between the ADD and the SUB routine; both consist of valid microinstructions, and nothing in the microprogram itself says which instruction it belongs to.

check.question: Name the two registers of a microprogrammed control unit and the two jobs of the unit.
check.answer: The control address register (which microinstruction) and the control data register (the microinstruction itself). The jobs are generating the control signals from the word, and sequencing - choosing the next address.
check.explanation: The first job is a wire from each bit to a control line; the second is the only real logic in the unit, which is why the design is described as simple.
